Remember this distinction: veterinarians treat disease, while Animal Scientists improve how animals are raised so they grow faster and stay healthier.

Not a good fit for people who are sensitive to blood or odors, avoid dirty environments, or only want office work. Animal science requires both experimental animals and livestock settings, and a research career will not last without comfort in those places.

A common path is a bachelor's degree in animal science, livestock production, or veterinary technology; graduate study at the master's or doctoral level; research-assistant work at an institute or corporate R&D department; and gradually taking independent responsibility for research or development projects.

A good fit for curious people who enjoy experiments and are comfortable working at livestock facilities. If you can spend a full day at a microscope and also record observations in a swine barn, this career could suit you.

Animal scientists study animal nutrition, genetics, reproduction, growth, and health. Through experiments and data analysis, they improve feeding and management practices to make livestock production more efficient, higher quality, and more sustainable.

paragraphs: A typical research cycle starts with experimental design: define groups and measures and calculate the sample size. Scientists then run a feeding trial at a livestock operation, measuring body weight and feed intake every few days. Once enough data accumulates, they analyze it in the laboratory, run statistics, create figures, write a report, and discuss production implementation with the company.

In one sentence: design experiments, analyze data, develop solutions, and implement them on farms. Work includes animal nutrition and breeding research, feed formulation optimization, reproductive health management, data analysis, and technical extension.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 2,800 animal scientists were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to reach 2,900 by 2034, a net increase of about 100 jobs, with roughly 200 openings each year. Median annual pay was about $79,100 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace animal scientists, but it will reshape research. AI can handle genomic analysis, phenotype modeling, and literature mining, shifting people toward experimental design, interpretation, and industry application. Field observation of animal behavior and the ability to turn research into production practices remain especially difficult to replace.

paragraphs: A 5/10 score means about half of this occupation's work involves desk tasks and data, including statistics, modeling, and literature, all areas where AI is strong.

Moderate AI exposure does not mean high risk. The better AI handles data, the more the field needs scientists who understand operations and can translate findings into production. Research roles limited to statistical work face pressure, while professionals who combine science and industry gain value.

Study animal science, livestock production, or veterinary technology, build a strong undergraduate foundation, and join a laboratory early. In the AI era, combine statistics, genomics, and data modeling with hands-on livestock experience for the widest range of options.

Adopt AI analysis and genomic methods, shifting from running experiments toward designing them and interpreting data. Spend time at livestock operations to connect research with industry needs and strengthen both funding prospects and career opportunities.

With a life-science or agricultural background, start as a research assistant or in corporate R&D and focus on animal nutrition and data analysis. On your resume, explain the experiments you conducted and the production problems you solved; this is more persuasive than a long publication list alone.

Do not hire animal scientists based only on publication counts. Evaluate experimental design and examples of industry application. Candidates who use AI efficiently and willingly work at livestock operations deserve more resources.
